Grundsatz: Verbot von Verhaftung und Zwang

Laut Artikel 4 Absatz 3 des Gesetzes dürfen Behörden Medienschaffende sowie deren Mitarbeitende oder Familienangehörige nicht unter Druck setzen, um vertrauliche Informationen oder Informanten offenzulegen. Konkret untersagt das Gesetz folgende Maßnahmen zum Zweck der Quellenausforschung: [1, 2, 3]
Inhaftierung und Festnahme. Journalistinnen und Journalisten dürfen nicht verhaftet werden, weil sie die Aussage über ihre Informanten verweigern. [1, 2]
Sanktionen. Geldstrafen oder andere staatliche Sanktionen wegen verweigerter Quellenangaben sind verboten. [1]
Durchsuchungen und Überwachung. Redaktionsräume und Privatwohnungen dürfen nicht durchsucht und Kommunikationswege nicht abgehört werden, um an Quellen zu gelangen. [1, 2, 3]

Strenge Ausnahmen für Zwangsmaßnahmen

Das Gesetz sieht in Artikel 4 Absatz 4 zwar Ausnahmen vor, knüpft diese aber an hohe rechtliche Hürden. Eine Maßnahme wie eine Verhaftung oder Überwachung ist nur zulässig, wenn alle folgenden Bedingungen gleichzeitig erfüllt sind: [1, 2, 3]
Überwiegendes Allgemeininteresse. Die Maßnahme muss durch ein zwingendes öffentliches Interesse (beispielsweise die Abwehr schwerster Gefahren oder die Aufklärung schwerer Straftaten) im Einzelfall gerechtfertigt sein. [1, 2]
Verhältnismäßigkeit. Es darf kein milderes Mittel geben, um an die benötigten Informationen zu gelangen. [1, 2]
Richterliche Vorab-Genehmigung. Ein unabhängiges Gericht oder eine unabhängige Justizbehörde muss die Maßnahme im Vorfeld ausdrücklich genehmigen. [1]

UNISA’s invite to Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture.
Colleagues, comrades, and family members of the late Dr Neville Alexander have publicly released a formal letter of objection sent to the Vice-Chancellor of the University of South Africa (UNISA). The statement registers our deep dismay over the institution’s decision to invite Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture at the Lagoon Beach Hotel, Milnerton, Cape Town, on Wednesday, 18 November 2026.
A collective letter of objection has been submitted to the Vice-Chancellor of UNISA detailing the profound disquiet of Dr Neville Alexander’s colleagues, comrades, and family members (listed below) regarding the invitation extended to Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the UNISA Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture on 18 November 2026 in Milnerton, Cape Town.
We submitted this appeal three days ago (as soon as we became aware of the invitation to Mr Manuel) with due respect for the office of the Vice-Chancellor and UNISA’s role in preserving our nation’s intellectual heritage. However, our overriding duty is to safeguard the integrity of Dr Alexander’s political and intellectual legacy - a legacy that stands fundamentally irreconcilable with the policy record of the invited speaker.
Even a cursory engagement with Dr Alexander’s writings, speeches, and lifelong praxis - spanning political economy, racial capitalism, imperialism, internationalism, the national question, national liberation as distinct from nationalism, and language policy - exposes an unbridgeable chasm between his social vision and that of Mr Manuel. These are not minor disagreements over strategy or tactics; they represent diametrically opposed worldviews on the very nature of society and structural transformation. To place Mr Manuel at the podium of a lecture bearing Dr Alexander’s name is to obscure the principled struggles that defined his life.
In our correspondence, we urged: “We trust that you will give this urgent matter your serious consideration, and we would deeply value the opportunity to engage with you further on this issue. Given the immediacy of the event (Wednesday, 18 November 2026), we kindly request a response at your earliest convenience, and no later than the morning of Monday, 16 November.”
We received a response from the Office of the Registrar this afternoon confirming that the event will proceed unchanged. The Registrar cited advanced logistical preparations to justify declining our appeal, offering a pledge of future consultation and a post-lecture meeting. Mindful of UNISA’s refusal to reconsider, we are compelled to place our objection on the public record.
Letter to Professor Puleng LenkaBula, Principal and Vice-Chancellor of the University of South Africa (UNISA).
RE: Our objection to the invitation of former Finance Minister Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver UNISA’s Neville Alexander Memorial lecture at the Lagoon Beach Hotel, Milnerton, Cape Town scheduled for the 18th of November 2026, at 6 pm.
Dear Professor LenkaBula,
We write to you as close colleagues, comrades, and the life partner of the late Dr Neville Alexander to express our profound disquiet about the invitation extended to Mr Trevor Manuel to deliver the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture.
Our objection is informed by our intimate knowledge of Dr Alexander's political convictions, intellectual commitments and lifelong struggle for a society founded on social justice, equality and genuine economic emancipation.
We believe that the invitation raises fundamental questions about the meaning, purpose and integrity of a memorial lecture established in honour of someone whose political and intellectual positions were so sharply at odds with the policies associated with Mr Trevor Manuel.
Dr Alexander's political and intellectual legacy cannot be separated from his opposition to neoliberalism and the socio-economic trajectory adopted by successive post-apartheid governments.
As a former political prisoner on Robben Island, a revolutionary socialist and humanist, an educator and a committed scholar-activist, Alexander dedicated his life to the struggle for a fundamentally different South Africa. His understanding of liberation went beyond the attainment of political democracy in 1994. He believed that genuine freedom required the transformation of the material, social, political and psychological and cultural conditions of the majority of our people, particularly the working class and the poor.
He was among those who warned that political liberation without meaningful socio-economic transformation would leave the structures of inequality largely intact and perpetuate corruption and cronyism. The persistence of mass unemployment, poverty, inequality and the concentration of economic power in post-apartheid South Africa gives continued relevance to the questions he raised.
Our objection to Mr Manuel is not personal. It is rooted in the political and intellectual commitments that Dr Alexander held throughout his life, and which the memorial lecture is meant to honour. Dr Alexander was unambiguous in his opposition to the neoliberal trajectory embarked upon by the post-apartheid establishment in the 1990s. He exposed the links between racism and capitalism and consistently argued that the ANC’s embrace of market fundamentalism betrayed the struggle’s emancipatory promise. He did not shy away from naming the architects of that betrayal.
Mr Manuel is one such architect. As Minister of Finance, he was the political face of the Growth, Employment and Redistribution (GEAR) strategy - a policy framework that Alexander and other anti-capitalist scholar-activists correctly identified as a neoliberal programme prioritising cuts in social and cultural spending, privatisation, and trade liberalisation. Unlike Mr Manuel, Dr Alexander maintained an uncompromising opposition to the precepts of the Washington Consensus.
GEAR was designed to reassure capital and serve the needs of large corporations. GEAR’s ostensible ‘trickle-down’ benefits, such as increased employment failed dismally. Dr Alexander’s critique was never merely abstract; it formed the very bedrock of his intellectual, organisational, and political praxis, serving to forge concrete alternatives to widespread immiseration. He remained until his death - eleven days after the Marikana Massacre - a revolutionary socialist and humanist who rejected the idea that the poor should bear the costs of market fundamentalism.
The contradictions surrounding Mr Manuel's invitation are not confined to his tenure as Minister of Finance.
Mr Manuel also went on to occupy senior leadership positions in the corporate financial sector. The symbolism of Mr Manuel’s later roles in corporations that embody the very neoliberal order Neville fought - makes this invitation even more inappropriate. To have him deliver a lecture in Dr Alexander’s name would be to turn a profound legacy against itself. It would suggest that the radical critique he advanced can be safely ignored, or worse, that the memorial lecture has become a platform for the very forces he spent his life opposing.
We are not suggesting that Mr Manuel should be denied the right to express or defend his economic and political positions. Nor are we opposed to robust intellectual debate. On the contrary, we believe that such debate is essential.
Our concern is that the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture should not become an occasion for the normalisation or uncritical celebration of political and economic positions that Alexander himself spent considerable intellectual energy challenging.
We must ask: What does it mean to honour Dr Alexander by inviting someone whose economic and political policy legacy was fundamentally opposed to the principles and aspirations that informed Dr Alexander's political thought?
Is this an attempt to depoliticise Dr Alexander's legacy and turn him into a ‘respectable’ academic figure, stripped of the radical politics that defined his life's work?
Are we now expected to commemorate Dr Alexander while overlooking the very political and socio-economic struggles that shaped his intellectual contribution to South African society?
We find this deeply troubling.
As people who knew, worked with, and struggled alongside Dr Alexander, we cannot remain silent when his name and legacy are invoked in ways that risk obscuring the political positions he consistently defended.
We recognise that universities must provide spaces for competing ideas and intellectual disagreements. However, there is a difference between hosting a debate about Dr Alexander's ideas and inviting a prominent political and corporate figure to deliver a memorial lecture without adequately accounting for the fundamental contradictions between his policy record and Dr Alexander's political convictions.
Professor LenkaBula, we therefore appeal to you, as Principal and Vice-Chancellor of Unisa, to intervene and reconsider this invitation.
Unisa is a vital public intellectual institution with a responsibility to uphold critical scholarship, intellectual integrity and historical accountability. Its role in preserving and advancing the legacies of South African intellectuals should not be reduced to hollow memorialisation and superficial ceremonial commemoration.
We accordingly call upon you and the relevant university structures to:
Reconsider Trevor Manuel's appointment as the speaker for the Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture.
Engage and consult with Dr Alexander's close colleagues and comrades before making decisions concerning the interpretation and public commemoration of his intellectual and political legacy – as the UNISA Western Cape colleagues respectfully did until last year.
Ensure that any memorial lecture bearing Dr Alexander's name reflects the radical intellectual traditions, political commitments and social justice principles that informed his life's work.
Establish an appropriate process through which those closest to Dr Alexander can contribute to safeguarding the integrity of his legacy.
We wish to emphasise that this intervention is not motivated by personal animosity towards Mr Trevor Manuel. It is motivated by our responsibility to protect the intellectual, political and historical integrity of Dr Alexander's legacy.
Dr Alexander was not someone who believed that all political and economic positions were equally compatible with the struggle for emancipation. He held firm convictions and was prepared to challenge those in power, including the leadership of the post-apartheid government, when he believed that their policies betrayed the aspirations of the liberation struggle. Dr. Alexander’s steadfast principles came at a steep personal cost, making him a target of the ruling establishment both during the apartheid era and in the years following 1994.
We cannot celebrate Dr Alexander’s courage and intellectual independence while remaining silent about the contradictions inherent in this invitation.
Dr Alexander's legacy must not be sanitised, depoliticised or appropriated in ways that contradict the very principles for which he struggled.
His memory deserves more than a prestigious lecture bearing his name. It deserves intellectual honesty, political integrity and fidelity to the unfinished struggle for social and economic emancipation.
We are also deeply mindful of Dr Alexander’s association with UNISA. It was through UNISA that he continued his studies while imprisoned on Robben Island, earning a BA Honours in History in 1969, and he became a tutor to other UNISA-enrolled inmates. UNISA later inaugurated the annual Neville Alexander Memorial Lecture in his honour, recognising his contribution to multilingualism and his lifelong commitment to education as a tool of liberation. For UNISA to host a speaker whose political, economic and social orientation to the oppressed and exploited contradicted everything that Neville's life and work represented, would undermine the integrity of that institutional legacy. The university has a responsibility to protect the political and ethical meaning of the memorial it established.
We therefore call on UNISA to withdraw the invitation to Mr Manuel, or on Mr Manuel to decline the invitation in recognition of the contradiction it represents. We ask that the lecture be used instead to reaffirm Dr Alexander’s actual legacy: his opposition to racial capitalism, his insistence that another world is possible, and his unwavering commitment to the poor and marginalised of South Africa. Anything less would be a disservice to his memory and to the struggle to which he gave his life.
We remain committed to defending Dr Alexander’s legacy, and we will continue to speak out whenever it is invoked in ways that contradict the principles he held.
We trust that you will give this matter the serious consideration it deserves and engage with us before proceeding with the proposed lecture.
Yours sincerely,
Close colleagues, comrades, family members and the life partner of the late Neville Alexander
On behalf of many others committed to preserving his intellectual, political and revolutionary legacy.

Pine Labs: A growing payments platform at an early-profit valuation

1.  What it does to make money 
Pine Labs sells the machines and software merchants use to take payments, then earns more as money flows through them. It also runs prepaid and gift card programmes for brands. Revenue splits into two platforms : 
DITP ₹532 Cr · 66%
IAP ₹275 Cr · 34%

DITP: merchant-side infrastructure (+21% YoY)
        a. POS terminals (22.3 lakh digital checkout points) earn subscription plus a take rate. Subscription is now 27% of total revenue.
        b. Fintech infrastructure: APIs for bill payments and data, paid per transaction (37 Cr in Q2, +33% YoY).

IAP: issuing and acquiring (+31% YoY)
Processing for prepaid and gift cards (management claims 80–85% of that market), plus distribution of cards for brands, interest on float and breakage income. Distribution carries lower margin (company: IAP contribution margin 52–55% vs 81–83% for DITP) so mix shifts move the blended 72–75%.

2 · Impact of MDR on UPI (Talk of the town)
Today, merchant UPI payments carry zero MDR (merchant discount rate), so Pine Labs earns nothing on roughly 70–77% of the transactions on its terminals. Under NPCI’s proposed framework, payments above ₹2,000 would carry a 0.4% (40 bps) MDR. Management expects about 11 bps to reach the acquirer layer and aims to keep 9–10 bps. The rollout is deferred pending regulatory clarity; the CEO said the ball is “completely in NPCI’s court”.

Annual MDR income is projected as  ~₹140 Cr a year. 

3.  Q2 FY27 results and consistency

Revenue: steady double-digit growth: +18%, +24%, +17%, +20%, +24% in the last five YoY readings. Q3 is seasonally strongest, Q4 dips.
Profit: the turn from losses to profit is real, but lumpy. PAT went ₹59 Cr → ₹20 Cr → ₹39 Cr over the last three quarters, swinging with tax and margin.
Margins: adjusted EBITDA margin has moved 23% → 21% → 17% → 19%. Contribution margin slid from 77% to 73% on distribution mix.
International revenue share dipped to 15% (from 17%) after a large retailer exited Singapore gift-card distribution.

4.  Guidance given
FY27 revenue growth : Higher than the 23–23.5% talked about at the start of the year
FY27 adj. EBITDA margin : “At least” 21%; H2 EBITDA much higher than H1

H1 FY27 revenue was ₹1543 Cr (+22% YoY). 
Reaching +23.5% for the year needs H2 growth of about 25%, against a strong Q3 base (₹744 Cr). 

H1 adj. EBITDA margin was ~18.2%; a 21% full-year result needs roughly 23% in H2, versus ~22% in H2 FY26. So both targets require H2 to beat H1.

What to track : 
Q3 revenue growth against the ~25% needed; whether H2 margin reaches the low 20s; NPCI’s final MDR decision; operating cash flow relative to the 13–15% working-capital band; and the tax rate trending to 30%.
Not a recommendation. DYOR

UPI / MDR / Paytm / Pine Labs

Agree. Sometimes we spend so much time looking at the P/E that we forget to ask how people are actually using the product and whether that is changing.

A company can still be making money and paying dividends, but have fewer opportunities to grow than it did earlier. In that case, a lower P/E may be justified. We can’t assume it will go back to its old valuation just because it looks cheap against its own history.

This is also what interests me about businesses like Pine Labs and Paytm. Think about the problems a shopkeeper has beyond accepting a payment. Which customer paid? What was the payment for? Has the money reached the bank? Can the customer buy on EMI? How much time goes into sorting all this out at the end of the day?

Someone made a very good point on my Pine Labs post: a jeweller running a gold savings scheme wants to know which of the day’s UPI credits came from scheme customers. That is a real problem. If you solve it properly, there is a reason for the merchant to pay you and keep using your service.

With Paytm too, I’d be more interested in whether merchants keep paying for its devices and services, and whether the company can earn more from those relationships over time. Just saying “UPI transactions are growing” doesn’t tell us enough about what shareholders will earn.

Of course, you can get the change in behaviour right and still overpay for the stock. And cash businesses may have more life left in them than the market assumes.

But the broader point stands. Before calling something cheap or expensive, it helps to spend some time understanding what customers are doing. The spreadsheet can look very precise even when our assumption about the next ten years is wrong.

Hitachi: Has Optimism Overshot? Shares Surge Over 10% on 64% Revenue Growth and 86% Jump in Orders, but Margin Miss and a 91x FY27 P/E Raise Valuation Concerns

Core Theme 
Hitachi Energy is delivering 64% revenue growth, an 86% jump in orders and a ₹33,300-crore backlog, with exports, services and data centres broadening the story, but a margin miss and a 91x FY27 multiple after a 73% rally leave the stock exposed to any slip in margins or HVDC execution.

Q2 FY27 Results: Strong Top Line
Shares of Hitachi Energy India surged over 10% on Friday, after the company reported another quarter of strong revenue growth and order inflows, with upbeat management commentary on growth outlook

Revenue rose 64% year-on-year to almost ₹3,000 crore in the September quarter, aided by strong execution; this follows 69% revenue growth in Q1

Ebitda, excluding foreign exchange impact, grew at a slower 55% to ₹462 crore, impacted by higher material costs and an adverse product mix

In Q1, Ebitda growth was far higher at 158%, aided by improved operating leverage and a favourable base

Total inflow in Q2 jumped 86% Y-o-Y to ₹4,100 crore, taking the order backlog to ₹33,300 crore, or around 3.2 times trailing twelve months revenue

Growth Outlook
Investors can expect near-term revenue growth to sustain, aided by a ramp-up in execution of high-voltage direct current (HVDC) projects and higher revenue recognition from these orders

Beyond the near term, growth should be supported by continued investments in transmission infrastructure and rising demand from data centres and battery energy storage systems (BESS)

Management indicated on the Q2 earnings call that four to five HVDC projects could be awarded over the next 12-24 months

Amid robust demand, management sees business visibility extending at least to 2035

Rising share of exports and services, along with improved operating leverage, should support profitability

Export orders rose 41% Y-o-Y in Q2, contributing 25-30% of total order inflow; these orders typically fetch 300-400 bps higher margins than domestic orders

The services business order inflow grew 77%, accounting for around 7% of total inflows, while railways, metro and renewables saw some moderation

Hitachi introduced a pre-engineered grid-to-rack solution to shorten data centre execution timelines

It is undertaking capex of ₹4,000 crore, including a ₹2,000 crore greenfield facility for large transformers at Karjan in Gujarat; most projects are expected to be completed by 2028, with a focus on technology localization

Margin Story
Hitachi’s Ebitda margin stood at 16.1% in H1 FY27 and 15.4% in Q2 FY27 (versus 15.4% in FY26 H1 per Mint’s text), with the Q2 margin missing estimates

Higher input costs and HVDC project execution could weigh on gross margins in the near term

Motilal Oswal Financial Services expects operating leverage and a higher share of exports and services to offset lower gross margin in HVDC projects; it is factoring in an Ebitda margin of 16.9%, 18.0% and 18.5% over FY27, FY28 and FY29

Jefferies India: “We believe 30%+ revenue growth continuing should see operating leverage-linked margin expansion of 760 bps over FY26-29 to 23%”; it expects earnings per share to grow at a 54% CAGR over this period

Investors will closely watch how margin recovery pans out

Valuation: Has Optimism Overshot?
Hitachi’s shares have gained 73% so far in 2026, and trade at 91 times estimated FY27 earnings, according to Bloomberg

A rise in competitive intensity due to industry-wide capacity expansion, or a delay in HVDC order execution, could lead to higher costs and margin erosion, acting as a dampener for the stock

Valuation may have entered an overheated zone

The Nifty IPO index has returned 21% this year on the back of Lenskart, Groww, Meesho and other new-age listings, but a 93x P/E dominated by loss-making, richly valued names, concentrated top weights and listing-price-based tracking lead experts to caution that investors may be better off picking individual IPOs.

The Performance: Recent Listings Lead
It has been a tough year for investors, and even though largecap indices were down, midcaps gave good returns; the real winners have been firms that listed over the last two years, which have managed to give some of the best returns in the market

Most of these issues were at least partly offers for sale (OFS), where private equity investors were looking for exits and in some cases promoters also saw an opportunity to sell some shares

The Nifty IPO index closed at 2,473.30 and the BSE IPO index at 19,618.43 on Friday

The Nifty IPO index gained 21.41% year-to-date this year and 16.85% over a one-year period; it is up 18.40% in six months, 5.50% in three months and 4.13% in a week

Over the long run, ecommerce and asset management company sectors, which dominate the index, are expected to grow the fastest

Heavyweights: Nifty IPO Index View
Lenskart Solutions: LTP ₹727.0; weight 10.22%; market cap ₹1.26 trn; 1-year return 81.7%

Groww: ₹225.0; weight 10.18%; ₹1.41 trn; 63.4%

Meesho: ₹257.1; weight 8.2%; ₹1.19 trn; 51.1%

ICICI Pru Asset Management: ₹3,040.4; weight 6.4%; ₹1.50 trn; 17.6%

INDO-MIM: ₹1,276.4; weight 3.91%; ₹0.63 trn; 72.1%

Lenskart is up 82% with a weight of 10.2% in the index; Groww is up 63% and Meesho up 52%; Shadowfax Technologies has been the best performer among the top weights, with a return of 158%

The index’s top 10 constituents account for about 52.8% of the index, per NSE Indices’ factsheet as of October 30; the four biggest weights together make up about 35.1%

Valuation Concerns
Per NSE Indices’ factsheet, the index’s price-earnings (P/E) ratio was 93.51 and price-to-book (P/B) was 8.84 on October 30, meaning the P/E has risen about 17% in two weeks; as of Friday, it has seen the sharpest expansion in P/E among the indices tracked

The P/E makes the index expensive because some of the initial public offerings (IPOs) trade at very high valuations: Physicswallah is the most expensive, at about 401 times earnings, followed by Lenskart Solutions (about 160 times) and Pine Labs (about 126 times)

Of 127 recently listed stocks with available issue prices, 88 trade above their issue price and 39 below; the median stock is up 24%, and 16 have at least doubled

Of 126 stocks with listing-day closing prices, 74 now trade above those levels; the median gain over the listing-day close is 7.5%

Longer-term returns are more modest, as NSE data showed the index has delivered a five-year price return of 4.46% a year and 8.70% since its January 2017 base date

Expert Views: Caution
Geetanjali Kedia, IPO expert at SPTulsian Investment Advisers: “We would not recommend investors put their money in an IPO index. This is primarily because the index would track the performance of these companies from their listing price rather than their issue price. It means investors would miss out on the listing gains in many of these IPOs”; investors are better off applying for quality companies rather than investing in a broad-based index

Kedia feels that investors can miss potential upsides due to quarterly rebalancing

Abhay Agarwal, founder and fund manager, Piper Serica: “The IPO market performance is directly related to secondary market performance, and that has been recovering. There is always room for good companies to go public and list... Some loss-making companies have dragged up the P/E multiple, particularly the larger-sized new economy IPOs. The IPO index has high weightage on these firms which makes the index look more expensive. But the P/E would be fairer if you take them out of the picture”

Mahindra Finance to Cut Mobility Loan Share, Scale Up Newer Segments by FY31: MD & CEO Raul Rebello Targets 16-18% AUM Growth Annually, RoA of 2.2-2.5% and Mobility Share Down From 80-85% to ~70%; AUM Could Exceed ₹3 Trillion

Core Theme
Mahindra Finance is working to reduce its reliance on mobility loans, from about 80-85% of the book to roughly 70% by FY31, by scaling secured housing and MSME lending, targeting 16-18% annual AUM growth and 2.2-2.5% RoA while avoiding unsecured loans, diversifying funding beyond banks and holding buffers against El Niño and drought risks.

Diversification: Why and Where
Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services (Mahindra Finance) is looking to reduce its dependence on vehicle financing by expanding into affordable housing and secured lending to micro and small enterprises

Raul Rebello, MD and CEO (interview with Aathira Varier, Subrata Panda and Manojit Saha): the franchise has a strong position in rural and semi-urban mobility, and protecting that remains the priority

Operating predominantly in one segment naturally limits long-term growth potential, so diversification has to be value-accretive

Two adjacent segments identified: affordable housing and select prime-mortgage lending, and secured lending to micro and small enterprises, since many mobility customers are entrepreneurs, transporters, single-vehicle operators and small business owners

The strategy is largely focused on secured lending; the company remains committed to a secured model and does not intend to enter unsecured lending

On gold loans: an attractive asset category, but there are concerns around business volatility and competition has intensified with several players entering; the company will evaluate costs and returns before entering

Growth Targets: FY27-FY31
The company has doubled its loan books from around ₹60,000 crore to ₹1.30 trillion under the FY31 plan and improved asset quality, though it fell short of its targeted net interest margin

For FY27-31, it is targeting 16-18% annual compounded AUM growth, credit costs within 1.3-1.7% and RoA of 2.2-2.5%

Medium-term goal: return on equity of 15%, with scope for further improvement through leverage

Between FY27 and FY31, the share of mobility in the portfolio is expected to decline from 80-85% to about 70%, with the balance increasingly contributed by newer segments

Today, more than 80% of business is concentrated in the wheels and mobility segment; as a scaled player, growth in the mobility portfolio will broadly track the underlying industry opportunity, with faster growth from newer businesses, particularly mortgages and MSME lending, which have a longer growth runway

At a 16-18% compounded growth rate, loan books could exceed ₹3 trillion by FY31

Risks: Weak Monsoon and El Niño
Targeted credit-cost range of 1.3-1.7% and the business model have the capacity to withstand even a weak monsoon

The company has built additional provisions of around ₹852 crore as buffer against potential downcycles, including an adverse El Niño outcome

It has also strengthened its liquidity, with a buffer of around ₹17,000 crore, which provides flexibility even if funding conditions tighten

Drought in certain states: no stress seen so far

Funding Strategy
The RBI has been encouraging NBFCs to diversify funding; Mahindra Finance’s objective is to diversify through retail deposits and capital markets while optimising cost of funds

Bank borrowings are around 51% of the funding mix; the company wants to look beyond direct bank loans to instruments such as non-convertible debentures, securitisation and direct assignments

The deposit-taking licence provides another source of funding, and focus on deposits is being stepped up

Banks will remain an important source for structural reasons: the company is the largest tractor financier and a leading used-vehicle financier, giving banks access to a substantial pool of priority-sector lending assets they are eager to hold

Insurance Distribution and IRDAI Paper
On the IRDAI consultation paper: the company participates in the insurance-revenue pool in several capacities and is moving towards insurance manufacturing, having submitted views to the regulator

Its central argument: expanding insurance coverage, ensuring fair policies and improving claim settlements require a broader focus than commissions alone

Distribution involves more than selling a policy; it includes advising customers and helping them choose suitable products

With a significant presence in rural and semi-urban markets, the company understands the cost of serving these customers and has called for appropriate commission rates and a phased implementation; rural and semi-urban markets may require somewhat higher commissions to support the broader objective of “Insurance for All by 2047”

Oswal Pumps Ltd - Q2 FY27 Results

1. Financial Performance -
- Revenue stood at ₹506.3 Cr, up 6.9% QoQ.
- Operating EBITDA was ₹57.5 Cr, with a margin of 11.3%.
- PAT stood at ₹39.6 Cr, with a margin of 7.7%.
- Margins were impacted by higher prices of aluminium, solar glass, copper, zinc and steel, particularly on older fixed-price contracts. Higher employee costs and EPC-related expenses also affected profitability.

2. Business Updates -
- Executable solar pump order book stands at 9,487 pumps, with an additional pipeline of 10,000 pumps across PM-KUSUM, Magel Tyala and exports.
- PM-KUSUM 2.0 has been delayed. Management expects its announcement within CY2026, but meaningful revenue contribution is expected only from Q1 FY28.
- The company is diversifying into rooftop, utility-scale and C&I solar EPC. Combined order book stands at 143 MW, with an additional pipeline of 168 MW.
- EPC business is expected to generate 12–15% operating EBITDA margins with a payment cycle of 90–120 days, significantly better than government projects.

3. Backward Integration: Major Development
- Company approved a 1.2 GW TOPCon solar cell manufacturing facility with total capex of ₹455.85 Cr.
- Funding: ₹159.85 Cr from unutilised IPO proceeds and ₹296 Cr through debt.
- Commercial operations targeted for April 2028.
- The facility is expected to meet 75–80% of internal solar cell requirements.
- Management expects a 6–7 percentage-point improvement in blended EBITDA margins after the plant becomes operational.

4. Working Capital and Debt
- Net debt stood at ₹531 Cr; net debt/equity at 0.30x.
- Receivable days stood at 229 days and inventory days at 56 days.
- Outstanding receivables were ₹1,300 Cr, entirely from government and government-backed entities.
- ₹208 Cr was collected in early October, entirely from Maharashtra.

5. Management Guidance -
- FY27 revenue guidance maintained at ₹4,000–4,500 Cr despite missing the earlier Q2 growth guidance of 10–15% YoY.
- Management expects business performance to improve progressively in H2 FY27.
- Target is to generate more than 25% of total business from non-government verticals.
- PM-KUSUM 2.0 is expected to contribute meaningfully from Q1 FY28.
- Expected cash conversion cycle under PM-KUSUM 2.0 is 140–150 days.
- Management is very confident about FY28, supported by government orders, EPC diversification and backward integration.

6. Key Risks -
- Delay in PM-KUSUM 2.0 is affecting near-term revenue growth.
- High receivables of ₹1,300 Cr and a 257-day cash conversion cycle remain concerns.
- Raw material inflation and competitive bidding are putting pressure on margins.

Overall View -
The company is transitioning from a government-dependent solar pump business towards a diversified solar platform. The long-term strategy of EPC diversification and backward integration is positive. However, near-term growth, margins and cash flow remain under pressure. The key monitorables are PM-KUSUM 2.0 execution, government collections and EPC growth

Sammaan Capital Ltd – Q2 & H1FY27 | Concall Insights

Financial Performance
•Q2 AUM ₹59,188 Cr (+5.2% QoQ); loan book ₹46,482 Cr
•Q2 disbursements ₹6,278 Cr (+62% QoQ); H1 disbursements ₹10,123 Cr

•ROA improved to 1.5% from 1.3% QoQ; return on managed assets improved to 1.3% from 1.1%

AUM Growth & Disbursement Guidance
•FY27 AUM target maintained at ₹70,700 Cr versus ₹59,188 Cr in Q2
•FY27 loan book target ₹53,000 Cr versus ₹46,482 Cr currently
•FY27 disbursement guidance ₹30,100 Cr, implying ~₹20,000 Cr disbursements in H2
•Management confident of achieving FY27 disbursement and profitability targets
•Growth strategy transitioning from balance-sheet stabilization to aggressive retail lending expansion
•Mortgage lending expected to remain the primary growth engine over the next two years, supported by new product launches

Cost of Funds & Margin Expansion
•Current cost of funds 9.8%; FY27 target ~9.3%
•Gross lending margin currently ~2.9%, with management targeting ~3.5%
•IHC backing, rating upgrades and access to international lenders expected to progressively reduce borrowing costs
•UAE banking relationship already providing >$150 Mn funding at competitive rates; another similar-sized transaction anticipated
•Company increased lending rates by 25 bps effective November, potentially improving near-term spreads
•Declining funding costs and higher-yielding retail products remain key drivers of NIM expansion and profitability
•Management targeting return on managed assets above 2% over time

Retail Lending & Product Diversification
•~94% of Q2 disbursements were secured loans, reflecting continued focus on asset quality
•Personal loans being expanded from purchased portfolios toward direct origination through branches
•Personal loan target ticket size ~₹2 lakh; indicative yields ~16–17%
•Business installment loans targeting MSMEs with ticket sizes of ₹18–20 lakh and yields of ~14–18%
•Gold loan soft launch planned across ~16 branches in Q3 FY27, followed by ~30 additional branches in Q4
•Gold loans targeting ~₹2 lakh ticket size and ~11–13% yields, with broader expansion planned in FY28
•Loan against securities, micro-LAP, rural housing finance and credit-fund partnerships provide additional AUM growth opportunities
•Higher-yielding products retained on balance sheet, while lower-yield mortgages increasingly originated and assigned to lenders

Distribution & Operating Leverage
•Branch network expanded from 217 to 245; FY27 target ~300 branches
•Expansion focused on Tier 2/3 cities and underserved semi-urban markets
•H1 employee additions ~1,123, largely dedicated to retail sourcing and branch operations
•Mortgage branches typically expected to break even within ~6 months; personal/business loan branches in ~4–6 months
•Gold loan branches expected to take ~12–18 months to break even
•Increasing branch productivity and technology-led processing expected to support operating leverage as disbursements scale

FY27–FY28 Earnings Growth Visibility
•H2 FY27 disbursements targeted at ~₹20,000 Cr versus ₹10,123 Cr in H1, creating significant AUM growth potential
•FY27 PAT target of ₹1,400 Cr implies approximately ₹844 Cr profitability requirement in H2
•Funding cost reduction from 9.8% toward 9.3% and margin expansion from 2.9% toward 3.5% offer key earnings upside
•Gold loans, personal loans and business loans expected to become additional growth engines from FY28
•Branch expansion and higher-yielding portfolio mix expected to improve long-term return ratios
•IHC-backed funding access, capital infusion and governance improvements support the company’s ambition to progress from AA+ toward AAA
•Key monitorables include H2 disbursement acceleration, cost-to-income ratio, new product asset quality and realization of funding-cost benefits
